amendments.rule: A **supplied subject** of a Greek infinitive — one Greek leaves unexpressed, which English must write — is a rule 7 helper on the **infinitive**, not on the finite verb governing it. `δοκεῖ … εἶναί τι` → *thinketh himself to be something* gives a bare *thinketh* to `δοκεῖ` and *himself to be* to the infinitive, as `ἵνα μὴ δόξω … ἐκφοβεῖν ὑμᾶς` → *that I may not seem … I would terrify you* gives *I terrify* to `ἐκφοβεῖν`, and `δοκεῖτε … ἔχειν` → *ye think that … ye have* gives *ye have* to `ἔχειν`. The infinitive is the verb whose subject it is, and rule 27 forbids splitting a helper from what licenses it. A supplied **object** is the contrast and it goes the other way, staying with the verb that requires it in English: `ἔχῃ … μεταδιδόναι` → *he may have whereof to give* and `ἔχωσιν … κατηγορεῖν` → *they might have whereof to accuse* keep *whereof* on `ἔχω`, both recorded `medium` conceding the infinitive. So the test is which verb the supplied word is an argument of. The **complementizer** is decided separately and belongs to the verb licensing the clause under rule 40, which is why JHN.5.39 gives *that* to `δοκεῖτε` while giving *ye* to `ἔχειν`; do not read the one placement off the other. Rule 11 does not bear on this: the ASV italicizes such a subject only sometimes, and its markup is evidence rather than a verdict. A **participle** is decided the same way and by the same test, the infinitive being named above only because it is the ordinary case and not because the rule is scoped to it. Where the participial clause leaves its subject unexpressed and the ASV writes one, that pronoun is a rule 7 helper on the **participle**, riding inside its unit along with any supplied subordinator under rule 86 and any supplied copula or auxiliary: `ἐλθόντων` → *when they were come*, `ἐλθόντα` → *when he came* and `εἰπόντος` → *when he said* each keep the supplied pronoun with the participle, as rule 86's own `ὄντες` → *when we were*, `ποιοῦντες` → *if ye do* and `ἐνεχθείσης` → *when there was borne* already read it. Where the clause **expresses** its subject — the genitive of a genitive absolute, or any noun or pronoun the Greek writes — that token takes the English subject word as its own `aligned` unit under rule 2, and the participle keeps only the subordinator, the copula and its own verb: `καταβαινόντων αὐτῶν` → *as they were coming down* gives *they* to `αὐτῶν`, as `Ἐλθόντων δὲ αὐτῶν` → *when they were come*, `Ἀναστρεφομένων δὲ αὐτῶν` → *while they abode* and `ἔτι αὐτοῦ λαλοῦντος` → *While he was yet speaking* do, that last leaving `ἔτι` its own *yet* besides. The English is often identical on both sides of that line — MAT.17.14 and MAT.17.24 both write *when they were come* — so decide it from whether the Greek expressed the subject and never from the English. That is rule 32's reasoning holding here: a word another source token has already written is spent, and nothing is left to supply.
amendments.why: MAT.17 renders 'when they were come' twice, at 17.14 with no expressed subject and at 17.24 with the genitive absolute's own autOn, and analyses them differently. The difference is correct and source-licensed, but rule 74 as it stood spoke only of infinitives, so nothing in the contract said where a participle's subject goes or that an expressed one takes the English word itself. The chapter reads it consistently across seven units (17.5, 17.9, 17.22, 17.24 expressed; 17.14, 17.25, 17.26 unexpressed), and rule 86's own cited units — ontes -> 'when we were', poiountes -> 'if ye do', enechtheisEs -> 'when there was borne' — already put a supplied subject on the participle, so the corpus corroborates rather than contradicts. Returned as an amendment rather than a new rule so that rule 74's scoping sentence is corrected where it stands instead of leaving an over-broad 'infinitive' for whoever reads it first.

conventions: mellei governing an infinitive and rendered by the English modal 'shall' is aligned to that modal as its own unit, and the infinitive stands alone on its lexical verb: MAT.17.12 mellei ... paschein -> 'shall ... suffer' and MAT.17.22 Mellei ... paradidosthai -> 'shall be delivered up'. The modal is what answers to mellei's own sense of impending action, not an auxiliary of the infinitive under rule 9, so do not fold it into the infinitive's unit.

kat' idian rendered by the single word 'apart' is one noncompositional unit under rules 45 and 94, headed on idian, at MAT.17.1 and MAT.17.19. Rule 93's judgment call is decided against rule 34's pleonastic arm here: idios by itself glosses 'one's own' and spells no part of 'apart', so the preposition is inside the English word and the pair joins rather than leaving kata unrepresented.

heOs pote rendered by 'how long' is one aligned unit taking both English words, headed on pote and on 'how', at both occurrences in MAT.17.17. This follows rule 64's display of the pair as a single item; splitting 'long' onto heOs and 'how' onto pote remains defensible and is recorded in the verse notes.

Versification split under rule 37 between MAT.17.14 and MAT.17.15: the projection places kai legOn at the head of 17.15, and the ASV translates it as 'and saying' at the end of 17.14. So 17.14 carries an added unit for 'and saying' headed on 'saying', and 17.15 leaves both kai and legOn as their own unrepresented units. A reference comparison reports 17.15 legOn as a disagreement, and that report is not a correction.

report: Checked all 42 candidate lemma groups and read the dump end to end for splits the table cannot see, it being keyed by source lemma and so blind to the chapter's single `added` unit. No genuine cross-verse split found, so patches is empty.

Articles: every treatment is licensed. Before a name -> unrepresented at 17.1 (twice), 17.4, 17.7, 17.9, 17.17, 17.18, 17.22, 17.25, 17.26 under rule 23; emptied by a possessive at 17.1, 17.2 (twice), 17.5, 17.8, 17.10, 17.15, 17.16, 17.20, 17.24, 17.25, 17.27 under rule 20; emptied by a demonstrative at 17.18 and 17.20 under rule 38; taking its own 'the' wherever the ASV writes a determiner. The 'of the' on the article at 17.25 against the bare 'the' at 17.5 and 17.9 is rule 21 holding, not a split: an expressed preposition takes its own English and leaves the article bare, an unaccompanied genitive does not.

Preverb particles under rule 106 are uniform: the particle rides inside the verb's unit at 17.1, 17.8, 17.9, 17.19, 17.22, 17.23, 17.25 and 17.27, and an expressed preposition keeps its own word beside it at 17.9 (ek -> from) and 17.18 (apo -> of). Both oblique arms are written and both are right: 'to him' rides with the dative at 17.14, 17.16 and 17.27, while the accusative objects of gonypeteo at 17.14 and prophthano at 17.25 stay bare with the preposition inside the verb.

Participle-to-finite junctures all sit on the verb they introduce (17.4, 17.7, 17.11, 17.17, 17.19, 17.27) under rule 88; supplied subordinators all sit on the participle (17.5, 17.6, 17.9, 17.14, 17.22, 17.24, 17.25, 17.26, 17.27) under rule 86. The four noncompositional idioms agree with each other and with the contract's own examples: kat' idian -> apart at 17.1 and 17.19, ei me -> save at 17.8, dia ti -> Why at 17.19, hina me -> lest at 17.27.

The near-miss worth naming: MAT.17.14 and MAT.17.24 both render 'when they were come', and 17.14 folds the supplied 'they' into the participle's unit while 17.24 gives 'they' its own unit on autOn. That is correct and source-licensed, 17.24 expressing the genitive-absolute subject where 17.14 does not, and the chapter reads it the same way at 17.5, 17.9, 17.22 (expressed) and 17.25, 17.26 (unexpressed). No rule states it, so it is returned as an amendment to rule 74 rather than left for the next chapter to rediscover.

BSB: none of the seven disagreements is an error, and no accepted edge was changed. 17.1 ton is an article before a name (rule 23); 17.8 tous, 17.10 hoi, 17.16 tois and 17.25 tOn are articles whose determiner slot a possessive occupies (rule 20), 17.10 on the selected reading r01 which supplies autou; 17.15 legOn is the rule 37 versification token, which rule 37 says in terms is not a correction; 17.26 ge is an emphatic particle for which the ASV writes no word, decided by the English-side test rules 65 and 70 apply to men, te and an intensifying kai, and the verse note already concedes the joined reading.

Not patched but flagged: MAT.17.8's unrepresented autOn cites rules 23 and 107, neither of which fits a bare intensive pronoun. The status is right on any reading. If r01 of SBLGNT.MAT.17.8.v008 omits the token, rule 97's mirror case is the correct citation and owes the fuller note that rule requires (unit id, reading carried, readings remaining); if r01 reads ton IEsoun, rule 23 is loosely right after all. I did not spend the evidence round on a note that changes no edge.
